#Question 1
```{r}
library(hexbin)
library(patchwork)
library(ggridges)
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
```

The data contains daily weather records from New York weather stations. It has `r (nrow(ny_noaa))` rows and `r (ncol(ny_noaa))` columns. Important variables include precipitation (tents of mm), snowfall (mm), snow depth (mm), minimum and maximum temperature (tents of degrees C), date of observation, and weather station ID. The data shows a specific station at a date in time from `r min(ny_noaa$date)` to `r max(ny_noaa$date)` across a number of `r n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` stations.

(missing data)

```{r}
noaa_clean <- ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = year(date),
    month = month(date),
    day = day(date),
    prcp = prcp / 10,                  #changing tenths of mm to mm#
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,      #changing tenths of degree C to degree C#
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,      #changing tenths of degree C to degree C#
  )
```

```{r}
snow_fall <- noaa_clean |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE)

```

For snowfall, the most commonly observed value is `r snow_fall$snow[1]` mm. This is because it does not snow often during the year such as during the summer, spring, and fall seasons. The next most commonly observed value is `r snow_fall$snow[2]` mm. This is because there are no data recorded for snow fall at a particular station. The next most observed value of snowfall is non-zero at `r snow_fall$snow[3]` mm.

```{r}
tmax_avg <- noaa_clean |>
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7) |>
  mutate(month_name = factor(month, levels = c(1,7), labels = c("January", "July"))) |>
  group_by(id, year, month_name) |>
  summarise(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r}
tmax_avg |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = .5) +
  geom_point(alpha = .5) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month_name) +
  labs(
    title = "Average daily maximum temperature by station in January vs July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean Maximum Temperature(C) ",
    caption = "NOAA Data"
  )
```
```{r}
july_outlier <- tmax_avg |>             #outlier in July#
  filter(month_name == "July") |>
  arrange(mean_tmax) |>
  head(1)
```

```{r}
january_outlier <- tmax_avg |>             #outlier in January#
  filter(month_name == "January") |>
  arrange(mean_tmax) |>
  head(1)
```

The average mean maximum temperatures are higher in July at around 25 degrees Celsius, and lower in January at around 0 degrees Celsius. This means that the average temperatures are lower in January than in July, which makes sense as it will be colder during the winter season of January versus the summer season of July. In addition, the range of mean maximum temperature values are larger in January with a range of about -10C to 10C, while in July the range is smaller from about 20C to 30C. As for outliers, for both months there are outliers for the coldest mean maximum temperatures. The lowest July mean temperature was `r round(july_outlier$mean_tmax,1)` degrees Celsius in `r july_outlier$year`. The lowest January mean temperature was `r round(january_outlier$mean_tmax,1)` degrees Celsius in `r january_outlier$year`. 

```{r}
tmax_tmin <- noaa_clean |>
  drop_na(tmax, tmin) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex(bins = 60) +
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis(option = "plasma", trans = "sqrt", name = "Count") +
  labs(
    title = "tmax vs tmin",
    x = "Minimum daily temperature (C)",
    y = "Maximum daily temperature (C)"
  )

snow_year <- noaa_clean |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  mutate(year = factor(year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) +
  geom_density_ridges(scale = .85) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year"
  )

tmax_tmin + snow_year
```
#Question 2
```{r}
covar_df =
  read_csv("./nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

accel_df =
  read_csv("./nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names()
```

```{r}
problem2_df =
  inner_join(covar_df, accel_df, by = "seqn") |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c(1,2), labels = c("male", "female")),
    education = factor(education, levels = c(1,2,3),
                       labels = c("less than high school", "high school equivalent", "more than high school"))
  )
```

```{r}
problem2_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```
The dataset has a total number of `r sum(problem2_df$sex == "male")` men and `r sum(problem2_df$sex == "female")` women. The largest education group is those with more than a high school level of education with a total number of `r sum(problem2_df$education == "more than high school")` men and women. Those with a high school equivalent education had the largest gap between the number of men and women, while the other education levels had almost an equal number of men and women. Among those with a high school equivalent education, there are a total number of `r sum(problem2_df$sex == "male" & problem2_df$education == "high school equivalent")` men and `r sum (problem2_df$sex == "female" & problem2_df$education == "high school equivalent")` women.

```{r}
problem2_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .7) +
  labs(
    title = "Age distribution of men and women in each education category",
    x = "Education",
    y = "Age (years)",
    fill = "Sex"
  )
```
The distribution of age for men and women that have an education level less than high school is fairly similar, with both sexes having a mean age of around 60 years. The distribution of age fom men and women that have an education level more than high school is also fairly similar, with both sexes having a mean age around 42 years. The most variation occurs in the high school equivalent education level. Men have a lower age distribution with a mean age of about 53 years, while women have a higher age distribution with a mean age of about 62 years. 

```{r}
problem2_total_df =
  problem2_df |>
  mutate(total_activity = rowSums(across(min1:min1440)))
```

```{r}
problem2_total_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex))+
  geom_point(alpha = .5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total activity by age (years)",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```
For participants with less than high school education, women aged less than 40 had higher total activity than men, however for those aged more than 40 years, men on average had higher total activity. For participants with a high school equivalent education, women had an average higher total activity across all ages greater than about 25 years. There is a large peak in total activity for women in this education level at around 40 years with a level of 17500 MMS. For those with more than high school education, women on average had higher total activity than men across all ages. For all education levels and sexes, total activity has an overall decrease as age increases.

```{r}
problem2_hour_df =
  problem2_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(minute),
    hour = minute / 60
  )

problem2_mean_df =
  problem2_hour_df |>
  group_by(education, sex, hour) |>
  summarise(mean_mims = mean(mims)) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{r}
problem2_hour_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = mims, color = sex, group = seqn)) +
  geom_line(alpha = .05) +
  geom_smooth(
    data = problem2_mean_df, 
    aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, group = sex),
    se = FALSE,
  ) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12, 18, 24))
  labs(
    title = "24-hour activity time courses by education and sex",
    x = "Hour",
    y = "MIMS",
    color = "Sex",
  )
  
```
For both men and women in all education levels, over a 24-hour time period, there is a similar level of mean total activity (MIMS). In addition, both sexes and all education levels follow a similar trend in MIMS over the course of 24 hours. Mean total activity drops close to 0 at around 6am, it peaks to about 12 MIMS at around 8am where it remains constant before it begins to decrease at around 8pm.

#Question 3
```{r}
jan_2020_df =
  read_csv("./Jan 2020 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = "2020", month = "January")

jan_2024_df =
  read_csv("./Jan 2024 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = "2024", month = "January")

july_2020_df =
  read_csv("./July 2020 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = "2020", month = "July")

july_2024_df =
  read_csv("./July 2024 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = "2024", month = "July")

citi_df = bind_rows(jan_2020_df, jan_2024_df, july_2020_df, july_2024_df)
```

```{r}
citi_df =
  citi_df |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    year = factor(year),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays, 
      levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")
    ),
    member_casual = factor(member_casual),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type)
  )
```
This dataset shows rides taken on NYC Citi Bikes in 2020 and 2024 of the months January and July. It has a total of `r nrow(citi_df)` rides and `r ncol(citi_df)` columns. Key variables included ride duration (`duration`), day of the week (`weekdays`), rider membership status (`member_casual`), and type of bike (`rideable_type`). 

```{r}
citi_df |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```
In total, there were `r sum(citi_df$member_casual == "member")` rides from members and `r sum(citi_df$member_casual == "casual")` rides from casual riders. The most rides occurred in July 2024 with a total of `r sum(citi_df$year == "2024" & citi_df$month == "July")` rides, with members having a larger number of rides compared to casuals.

```{r}
citi_df |>
  filter(year == "2024", month == "July") |>
  count(start_station_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(5) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Starting station", "Number of rides")
  )
```

In July of 2024, the most popular starting station was `r citi_df$start_station_name[52973]` with 163 rides. 
```{r}
citi_df |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarise(median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, color = month, group = month)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(. ~ year) +
  labs(
    title = "Median ride duration by day of the week, month, and year",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median ride duration (minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  )
```

In both 2020 and 2024, the median ride duration was higher in July vs January. In 2020, the median ride duration in July was around 15 minutes, with the highest median ride duration being on Saturday and Sunday at around 16 minutes. The median ride duration in January was around 8.5 minutes, with the highest median ride durations being on Saturday and Sunday at around 10 minutes. In 2024, the median ride times in January and July were lower than in 2020. In July, the median ride time was about 10 minutes, with the highest being on Saturday at around 11 minutes. In January, the median ride time was about 7.5 minutes with the highest day being Saturday around 8 minutes.

```{r}
citi_df |>
  filter(year == "2024") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = member_casual, y = duration, fill = rideable_type)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .7) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "sqrt") +
  labs(
    title = "Ride duration in 2024 by month, membership staus, and bike type",
    x = "Membership status",
    y = "Ride duration (minutes)",
    fill = "Bike type"
  )

```
Ride duration was fairly equal by bike type as classic and electric bikes have similar distributions. In January and July, casual riders had a longer ride duration than members. The mean ride time remained under 50 minutes, however there are many outliers of longer rides for each bike type.
